## Core principle: composition-first design

Every UI must be built **only** from components in the catalog below, following the **layer rules** (see *Layer rules* below — a component may import only from its layer's allowed layers, and the graph must stay acyclic).
**Never** assemble screens from ad-hoc HTML, random one-off JSX, or unrelated primitives.

Forbidden forever:
- Raw UI elements: `<div>`, `<button>`, `<input>`, `<a>`, `<span>`
- Inline styles (`style={{}}`) and arbitrary one-off CSS classes
- Inventing markup that bypasses the design system
- **Hardcoded design values** — raw `#hex` / `rgb()` / `hsl()` colors, `px`/`rem` spacing, one-off radii, shadows, font sizes, or magic numbers when a design token expresses them

---

## Build on design tokens (mandatory)

**Every visual value MUST come from a design-system token** (a CSS custom property), never a hardcoded literal. Tokens are the single source of truth — editing one in Gantry's **Tokens** tab updates every component at once. Hardcoded values silently break that contract.

Rules:
1. Colors, spacing, radii, typography, shadows, z-index, and motion **must** reference a token: `var(--token-name)`.
2. **Never** inline a literal (`#4f46e5`, `12px`, `0 1px 3px rgba(...)`) when a token already expresses it — use the token from the catalog below.
3. If the token you need **does not exist**: add it to the project's token file first (`:root { --token-name: value; }`), re-scan, **then** reference it with `var(--token-name)`. Do not hardcode the raw value as a shortcut.
4. Keep variant style maps keyed by `variant` / `tone`, but their values must be tokens:
   ```ts
   const styles = {
     primary:   { background: 'var(--color-primary)', color: 'var(--color-on-primary)' },
     secondary: { background: 'var(--color-surface)',  color: 'var(--color-text)' },
   }
   ```
5. Reuse existing tokens before inventing new ones. Only introduce a new token when no existing token fits its semantic role; name it by **purpose** (`--color-danger`), not by raw value (`--red-500`).

---

## Token architecture — semantic, layered, restrained

Good token systems are **small, semantic, and layered** — not a variable per value.

1. **Three layers; components consume only the semantic layer.**
   - *Primitive / reference* tokens hold the raw palette + scales (`--blue-600: #2563eb`, `--space-4: 16px`). Internal building blocks only.
   - *Semantic / system* tokens express **intent** (`--color-primary`, `--color-text`, `--color-text-muted`, `--color-border`, `--space-inset-md`). **Components use these.**
   - *Component* tokens are optional and rare — only when a value genuinely can't be expressed semantically.
   - **Never reference a primitive (`--blue-600`) from a component.** Reference the semantic token; the semantic token references the primitive — that is what makes theming (light / dark / brand) a one-place change.
2. **Name by role, not by value or component:** `--color-text-muted` ✔, `--gray-500` ✘ (value), `--button-bg` ✘ (component, unless it is a true component token).
3. **Use scales; reuse steps.** Spacing (4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 24 / 32…), the type scale, radii, and elevation all come from one small consistent ramp. Pick the nearest existing step — do **not** invent a one-off `--space-13`.
4. **A token must earn its place.** Create one only when the value is reused **or** encodes a real decision. Used once → use an existing scale step, not a new token. Fewer well-named tokens beat hundreds of ad-hoc ones.
5. **Consolidate duplicates.** Two tokens with the same value and overlapping meaning → merge into one semantic name.

---

## Fewer, better — component API restraint

**More variants and props is NOT better.** The best API is the *smallest* one that covers the real, recurring use cases. Every extra variant, prop, and boolean is permanent surface area to design, document, test, preview, and keep consistent. Bias toward **less**.

### Composition over configuration
- Prefer **slots / `children`** over configuration props: `<Card>{header}{body}{footer}</Card>` (or `header` / `footer` slot props) beats `<Card showHeader headerTitle headerIcon headerActions footerAlign … />`.
- If a need is a one-off, **compose it at the call site** — do not bake a new prop/variant into the component for it.

### Add a variant only when it earns it
Add a `variant` / `tone` / `size` value **only if all** hold:
1. It is a **semantic** distinction (e.g. primary vs secondary action), not a one-off visual tweak.
2. It is **reused** in ~3+ real places.
3. It can't be achieved by composing existing pieces.
Otherwise compose, or extend at the call site. **Delete** variants/props that aren't used — dead options are liability, not flexibility.

### Avoid combinatorial explosion
- N independent booleans = 2^N states to maintain and preview. Collapse mutually-exclusive booleans into **one enum**: `state: 'default' | 'loading' | 'disabled'` — not `isLoading` + `isDisabled` + `isActive` together.
- **One axis of meaning per prop.** Don't overload `variant` to mean colour *and* size *and* shape; split only into the axes that are separately, genuinely needed (often just `variant`; add `size` only if real).
- Lean on **sensible defaults** so the common case needs zero props.

### Decision: variant vs compose vs new component
| Situation | Do this |
|-----------|---------|
| Recurring semantic difference of the same thing (~3+ uses) | add a **variant** value |
| One-off visual need | **compose** at the call site / pass `children` |
| Different responsibility or structure | **new component** at the correct layer |
| Many flags toggling parts on / off | **split** into smaller composable components |

> Rule of thumb: prefer **3 small composable components over 1 component with 12 props**. Reach for the fewest variants and variables that still read clearly — restraint *is* the architecture.

---

## Build components systematically (maintainable by default)

Create UI **the same way every time** — predictable folders, readable props, and one clear job per component. If a teammate (or Gantry) opens the files, they should understand the component in under a minute.

### Folder & file system (one component = one module)

Every component lives in its own folder under the correct layer:

```
ComponentName/
  ComponentName.tsx          # implementation
  ComponentName.types.ts     # public props API (required)
  ComponentName.meta.ts      # optional: export const description = '...'
  ComponentName.variants.ts  # optional: gantryVariants for preview states
  index.ts                   # re-export
```

Rules:
- **One component per folder** — no shared grab-bag files.
- **Names match** — folder, files, export, and `ComponentNameProps` all use the same `ComponentName`.
- **Types live in `.types.ts`** — do not bury the public API inside the `.tsx` file.
- **Add `description`** in `.meta.ts` or JSDoc so Gantry and humans know *why* the component exists.

### Props must be human-readable (the public API)

Props are a **user interface for developers**. Name them like product copy, not like minified code.

**Do:**
- Use full words: `label`, `variant`, `isDisabled` (or `disabled`), `actionLabel`, `imageUrl`.
- Use string unions for visual choices: `variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost'` — not magic numbers.
- Keep prop count small (roughly **3–8** on leaf primitives, slightly more on composing components). If there are many knobs, split into another component or compose.
- Mark optional props with `?` and sensible defaults in the function signature.
- Document non-obvious props with a one-line JSDoc above the property in `ComponentName.types.ts`.
- Group visual tokens in named maps (`styles`, `tones`) keyed by `variant` / `tone` — not anonymous inline blobs.

**Don't:**
- Cryptic names: `t`, `v`, `cfg`, `data`, `opts`, `item` (when you mean `product` or `user`).
- Giant config objects: `options: { theme: ..., size: ..., flags: ... }` unless the component is a true layout engine.
- Boolean soup without meaning: five `showX` flags — prefer composition or a single `variant`.
- `any`, `unknown`, or overly wide types on the public API.
- Leaking implementation details as props (`classNames`, raw `style`, internal IDs) unless the design system explicitly allows them.

**Good vs bad examples:**

| Bad | Good | Why |
|-----|------|-----|
| `txt: string` | `label: string` | Reads like UI, not code |
| `type: 1 \| 2 \| 3` | `variant: 'primary' \| 'secondary'` | Self-documenting in Gantry & IDE |
| `onPress` + `onClick` duplicate | one `onClick?` | One obvious action |
| 12 optional booleans | 2–3 props + composition | Easier to preview and maintain |
| `variant` with 8 values, 1 used | `variant: 'primary' \| 'secondary'` + compose | Variants must be reused & semantic |
| `isLoading` + `isDisabled` + `isActive` | `state: 'loading' \| 'disabled' \| …` | Avoid 2^N boolean combinations |

### Behaviour & styling conventions

Layer roles in this project:
- **Primitives** (`primitive`) — leaf primitive (a single visual idea); imports nothing from the design system.
- **Components** (`component`) — composes from primitive / component; do not re-style raw HTML.

- **Styles** — keep variant colors in a `const styles` / `const tones` map at the top of the file; every value must be a design token (`var(--token)`), never a hardcoded literal.
- **Callbacks** — `onClick`, `onSubmit`, `onChange` only when needed; never required for preview.

### Checklist before considering a component "done"

1. Folder structure matches the template above.
2. Every prop name is obvious without reading the implementation.
3. `ComponentName.types.ts` exports `ComponentNameProps` with unions/booleans/strings Gantry can edit.
4. Default props render a meaningful preview (not an empty box).
5. `description` explains the purpose in one sentence.
6. Component is registered in the catalog after sync (correct layer, import path).
7. **API is minimal** — every variant and prop earns its place; no unused options, no boolean soup, composition preferred over configuration (see *Fewer, better*).
8. **Every visual value is a semantic token** (`var(--token)`) — no primitives, no literals (see *Token architecture*).

## When the user asks for UI (e.g. "user card", "profile block")

**Do not** improvise a new card from random elements. Follow this order:

1. **Match** — Search the catalog for an existing component that already solves the request (name, props, layer).
   - Example: "user card" → prefer **ProfileCard**, **Card**, or compose documented catalog components before creating anything new.
2. **Compose** — If no single component fits, build the UI by **combining existing** catalog components only.
3. **Gap analysis** — List each UI piece you need (avatar, title, actions, layout, etc.). Map every piece to a catalog component.
4. **Fill gaps bottom-up** — If something is missing, add the **smallest** missing component at the **lowest layer** that fits (often a `primitive`), sync, then compose upward. Never import upward or skip the layer rules.
5. **Last resort** — Only create a higher-layer component after all the lower-layer pieces it composes already exist.

Before writing code, briefly state: *matched component* OR *composition plan* OR *missing pieces to add (with layer)*.

---

## Creating ANY new component (mandatory workflow)

1. **Inventory** — Write the UI pieces required (text, image, actions, layout container, etc.).
2. **Map to catalog** — For each piece, pick an existing component from the list below. No piece may be left unmapped.
3. **Check layers** — a component may import **only** from the layers its own layer allows (see *Layer rules*):
- **Primitives** (`primitive`) — leaf primitive (a single visual idea); imports nothing from the design system.
- **Components** (`component`) — composes from primitive / component; do not re-style raw HTML.
4. **Add missing lower-layer pieces first** — Create `ComponentName/ComponentName.tsx` + `ComponentName.types.ts` under the correct layer folder, then re-scan.
5. **Compose** — Implement the new component using imports from the catalog only (same `importPath` style as siblings).
6. **No raw HTML** for UI structure — use catalog layout components (e.g. **Surface**, **Stack**, **Row**, **Text** if present) instead of `<div>` / `<span>`.

### Gantry preview & Customize (mandatory for every component)

Every component **must** work in Gantry preview and the **Customize** editor:

- Add `ComponentName.types.ts` with an exported `ComponentNameProps` interface (string/union/boolean/number props — not only `children`).
- Prefer a `styles` or `tones` map in `.tsx` with variant keys (`primary`, `secondary`, …). Every color/spacing value must reference a design token (`var(--token)`) — edit those values in Gantry's Tokens tab, not by hardcoding.
- Optional: `ComponentName.variants.ts` with `gantryVariants` for rich preview states.
- Layout wrappers (`Surface`, `Stack`, `Row`) may use `children`; Gantry injects default child text in preview — still add editable props (`padding`, `gap`, `variant`, etc.).
- Leaf primitives should expose at least one of: `label`, `text`, `title`, `variant`, `tone`, `size` so Customize always has fields.

Reject approaches that: mix random HTML, duplicate an existing component, jump to a higher layer when a lower-layer component already covers the need, import upward across layers, or ship unreadable prop names that only the author understands.

## Layer rules (strict)

This project has no layer folders, so Gantry uses **flat-library mode**: a component is a *primitive* if it imports no other catalog component, otherwise a *composer*. The only hard rule is **no circular dependencies**.

| Layer | Role | May import from |
|-------|------|-----------------|
| `primitive` | primitive (raw HTML OK) | nothing from the design system |
| `component` | composes catalog | primitive + component |

---

## Import convention

Use the exact `importPath` from the catalog, e.g.:

```tsx
import { Button } from '@/components/Example'
```
